sweep_summary: The sweep's only title-keyword item for narr1259 (Polo 2017, RESLA) is a study of Spanish L1 stress acquisition -- a 'longitudinal'/'acento' title-match, irrelevant, paywalled, priority none. Beyond that item I re-read the complete McDonald 1977 Yaraldi phonology thesis already held on file (sec. 2.4: primary stress on the first syllable, secondary on the 3rd and 5th, a closed set of equal-stress CaC-sonorant roots) and, via Google Books snippet feeds saved to, verified for the first time the actual wording of the catalog's deciding passage, Yallop 1975:59-60 ('the third syllable is also relatively stressed', with the nakun/kaykunun/po:li examples and the page number 60 in the snippet) and the Cə-word note (narinjari, wunuyi 'generally have stress on the first syllable' but informant K sometimes shifts it to the second syllable with the first vowel reduced to [ə]). The archive.org Rosetta 'detail' item proved to be sec. 1.1, not ch. 4; ch. 4 of Yallop 1975 remains print-only apart from snippets (medium priority to acquire for full verification, no coding change expected). Both first-hand sources confirm the catalog's fixed-strict initial-stress coding; nothing supersedes it. All fetched sources

new_statements.quote: Strong primary stress occurs on the first syllable of a word. Only in a few words is this pattern broken, and only on these is stress marked. Unstressed vowels are schwa [...]. In all words in which stress does not occur on the initial syllable, a fairly equal distribution of stress on first and second syllables may be observed. It appears that a shift of stress takes place over a single sonorant, yielding syllables with equal stress. [...] In disyllabic stems, the vowel of the second syllable is unstressed and often reduced. [...] Secondary stress occurs on the third syllable of a word, and apparently again on the fifth.
new_statements.citation: McDonald, Maryalyce. 1977. A study of the phonetics and phonology of Yaraldi and associated dialects. MA thesis, Australian National University. Sec. 2.4 Stress, pp. 25-26.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.4.1 Primary Stress and 2.4.2 Secondary Stress, printed pp. 25-26 (PDF pp. 32-33; text-layer lines 1466-1497)
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial primary stress with secondary stress on odd syllables (3rd, 5th), i.e. a left-to-right trochaic pattern; the only exceptions are a closed set of roots with equal stress on syllables 1-2 produced by stress shift over a single intervocalic apical sonorant. This is the same picture StressTyp2 draws from Yallop 1975:59-60, whose wording Google Books snippets now verify for the first time ('the third syllable is also relatively stressed'; Cə-words like narinjari, wunuyi 'generally have stress on the first syllable' but K sometimes shifts it to the second with the first vowel reduced to [ə]). Catalog coding fixed-strict (initial) is confirmed by both first-hand sources.

sources.note: Dedicated phonology study of the last speakers' tapes. Primary stress on the first syllable of a word; a small set of words (mostly CaC-roots with a single intervocalic apical sonorant) show equal stress on first and second syllables through a shift over the sonorant; secondary stress on the third and apparently fifth syllable; case suffixes unstressed, other monosyllabic suffixes take secondary stress, disyllabic suffixes stressed on their final syllable. Agrees with StressTyp2/Yallop 1975 -> fixed-strict initial stands.
